prompt: What does a language model produce at each step of generation?
hint: Look at what `lab/next.py` prints.

choices.text: The next word of the answer, chosen by looking it up in its training text
choices.why: Nothing is looked up, and the unit is a token rather than a word.

choices.text: A complete sentence, which is then cut into tokens for the user
choices.why: Sentences are built a token at a time; nothing is produced whole.

choices.text: A probability for every possible next token
choices.why: Right. Choosing one of them is a separate step.

choices.text: A score saying how true the text so far is
choices.why: Nothing in the loop measures truth, which is lesson 1 section 07's point.

prompt: After `If the file does not`, `tinylm` ranks ` exist` fourth, level with ` add` and ` close`. Why does a reader's obvious choice not win?
hint: `context used: 2 tokens`.

choices.text: It only sees `does not`, and in its corpus many words follow those two
choices.why: Right. Two tokens of context cannot tell which file sentence this is.

choices.text: Its corpus never contains the word exist
choices.why: It does: ` exist` is in the list, at 7.7%.

choices.text: Greedy decoding was switched off for `next.py`
choices.why: `next.py` does not decode at all; it prints the distribution.

choices.text: The leading space makes ` exist` a rarer token than `exist`
choices.why: The space is part of the token in every one of the five, so it cannot separate them.

prompt: The greedy run ends in `the type of the` repeated four times. What would stop that loop in this model?
hint: Greedy means the same context always gives the same token.

choices.text: A longer prompt, so the model has more text to continue from
choices.why: The loop starts after the prompt, and from then on only the last two tokens matter.

choices.text: More output tokens, so the loop has room to run its course
choices.why: More tokens are more repetitions.

choices.text: Another seed, keeping the temperature at 0
choices.why: At 0 there is no draw, so the seed is never used.

choices.text: Drawing from the distribution instead of taking the top
choices.why: Right. A draw can leave the loop the moment another token is picked.

prompt: In `Token|isation| is| not| splitting`, where does the space before `is` go?
hint: Read where the `|` falls.

choices.text: It is dropped, since tokenizers ignore whitespace
choices.why: The eight spaces of indentation in the code line are a token of their own, so whitespace is kept.

choices.text: Into the same token as `is`
choices.why: Right: ` is` is one token, space included.

choices.text: Into a token of its own, between `isation` and `is`
choices.why: There is no `| |` between them; the space is inside ` is`.

choices.text: At the end of `isation`
choices.why: The `|` falls before the space, not after it.

prompt: Under `o200k_base`, how many tokens is the Portuguese sentence `A tokenização não divide o texto nos espaços.`?
hint: The third line of the first capture.

prompt: `1290000` comes out as `129|000|0`. What does that tell you about asking a model to add up an order?
hint: What the model receives is the pieces.

choices.text: Nothing; the tokenizer joins the pieces back into a number before the model sees them
choices.why: The model receives token ids, and these are three of them.

choices.text: That prices should be sent with a decimal point, which tokenizes cleanly
choices.why: `.sub` shows that a dot is just one more piece to split at.

choices.text: The model never sees the number as a number, so do the sum in code
choices.why: Right. That is why the shop keeps money in code.

choices.text: Only that `o200k_base` is a poor choice; `cl100k_base` keeps numbers whole
choices.why: Both cut digits into groups; the section's point is about tokenizers in general.

prompt: You count a prompt with `tiktoken` and get 1,200 tokens. Who can you quote that number to?
hint: A count belongs to a tokenizer.

choices.text: Somebody using a model that `tiktoken` maps to the same encoding
choices.why: Right. For any other model it is an estimate.

choices.text: Anybody, since a token is the same unit for every provider
choices.why: `espaços` is one token in one encoding and two in another.

choices.text: Anthropic's billing team, since `tiktoken` follows their format
choices.why: Anthropic does not publish its tokenizer, and counts for you instead.

choices.text: Nobody; token counts are random and change on every run
choices.why: A tokenizer is deterministic: the same text always gives the same ids.

prompt: `shop/cart.py` is 265 tokens for 121 words, so code costs about ___ tokens a word, against one and a half for the corpus's prose.
hint: Divide, and round to a whole number.

prompt: What does a temperature of 0 do?
hint: Look at what the seed did at 0.

choices.text: It makes the model refuse uncertain answers
choices.why: Temperature only reshapes a distribution; it adds no refusal.

choices.text: It gives every token the same chance
choices.why: That is what a very high temperature tends towards.

choices.text: It turns off the context, so only the prompt is used
choices.why: The context is used the same way at every temperature.

choices.text: The top token always wins, which is greedy decoding
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A teammate's test sends the same prompt to a hosted model at temperature 0 and compares the reply to a saved string. It fails one run in thirty. What is wrong?
hint: What does the section say providers promise?

choices.text: The temperature should be 1, which is the default
choices.why: A higher temperature makes the reply vary more, not less.

choices.text: The test relies on a model repeating itself, which nothing guarantees
choices.why: Right. A test that needs a fixed answer should not call a model.

choices.text: The seed should be fixed, which makes every hosted model deterministic
choices.why: Where a seed is accepted at all, the providers call the result best effort.

choices.text: The prompt is too short for temperature 0 to take effect
choices.why: Temperature acts on every draw, whatever the prompt's length.

prompt: With top-p at 0.5, which tokens can be drawn?
hint: It is a share of the probability, not a count.

choices.text: The five most likely tokens, whatever their probabilities
choices.why: A fixed number of tokens is top-k.

choices.text: Any token whose own probability is above 50%, and no other
choices.why: There is rarely any such token; the cut is a running total.

choices.text: The likeliest tokens until they add up to half
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Half of the vocabulary, chosen at random before each draw
choices.why: The kept tokens are the most likely ones, in order.

prompt: What is an embedding, as the section uses the word?
hint: WordLlama returned one of them per text.

choices.text: One vector per text, placed by what the text is about
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A compressed copy of the text that can be decoded back into the words
choices.why: Nothing decodes 256 numbers back into a sentence.

choices.text: The list of token ids the tokenizer produced
choices.why: Those are integers indexing a vocabulary; an embedding is a direction in space.

choices.text: A summary sentence written by the model
choices.why: An embedding model writes no text.

prompt: For `the cart total is wrong`, WordLlama ranks `the cart page loads slowly` first. Why?
hint: What do the winner and the query share?

choices.text: A slow cart page is the most frequent cause of a wrong total at checkout
choices.why: They are two different problems; the section says the winner is wrong.

choices.text: Cosine similarity favours shorter sentences
choices.why: The winner is not the shortest candidate, and length does not enter the cosine.

choices.text: It shares `the cart`, and this small model leans on shared words
choices.why: Right. The rephrasings share almost no words and lose.

choices.text: The query was not normalised, so the scores are meaningless
choices.why: `similar.py` asks for normalised vectors with `norm=True`.

prompt: A support search finds the handbook passage about coupons for the question *can a coupon be used twice?* The passage says it cannot. What, from this section, is the embedding's part in getting the answer right?
hint: `was accepted` against `was not accepted`: 0.964.

choices.text: All of it, since a passage close to the question is a passage that agrees with it
choices.why: The closest match to *was accepted* was *was not accepted*.

choices.text: Finding the passage; whether it says yes or no has to be read by the generating model or a person
choices.why: Right. Embeddings place text by subject.

choices.text: None, because embeddings cannot find passages about coupons
choices.why: They found it; that part is what they are good at.

choices.text: Deciding the answer, as long as the score is above 0.9
choices.why: A score is a ranking, not a verdict, and 0.964 was the opposite statement.

prompt: Model A scores a pair of sentences 0.81 and model B scores the same pair 0.47. What can you conclude?
hint: The section says what a score can be compared with.

choices.text: Model A understood the pair better
choices.why: A higher number from another model is not a better reading of the same pair.

choices.text: Model B is broken, since 0.47 is below 0.5
choices.why: There is no threshold of 0.5; scales differ between models.

choices.text: The sentences mean 81% the same thing
choices.why: A cosine is not a percentage of sameness.

choices.text: Nothing, until you see how each model ranks other pairs
choices.why: Right. Compare scores only with scores from the same model.

prompt: How does a chat application make a model answer *how many items are in it now?* about a cart mentioned two turns earlier?
hint: Look at what the third request carried.

choices.text: The model keeps the first two turns in memory until the session ends
choices.why: The model keeps nothing between requests.

choices.text: It sends the whole conversation again with the new question
choices.why: Right. That is all memory is.

choices.text: The provider attaches the previous replies by itself
choices.why: In the capture, the list was built and sent by `turns.py`.

choices.text: It cannot; models answer one question at a time
choices.why: It can, by sending the history.

prompt: In `turns.py`, how many input tokens did the third turn carry?
hint: The third line of the capture.

prompt: Which of these share the context window with the conversation? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists what else a request carries.

choices.text: The system prompt
choices.why: Yes, it is text in the request.

choices.text: The model's training data
choices.why: Training data is not sent; it shaped the parameters long before.

choices.text: Tool definitions
choices.why: Yes, they are counted like everything else.

choices.text: The reply the model is about to write
choices.why: Yes: input and output share one window.

prompt: An assistant writes code for `requests` 2.x in a project that pins `httpx` and never imports `requests`. The assistant was not shown the dependency file. What does the section's working rule say about this?
hint: If it is not in the request…

choices.text: The assistant is faulty, since it should know which libraries the project uses
choices.why: It can only know what it was sent.

choices.text: The model should be retrained on the project
choices.why: Training is not how a project's facts reach a model in practice.

choices.text: Nothing; assistants read the whole repository by themselves
choices.why: Only what a tool puts in the context; lesson 3 shows what an editor gathers.

choices.text: It guessed, because the fact that decides the answer was not in its context
choices.why: Right. Put the dependency file in the context.

prompt: The day a model's training text stops is called its training ___.

prompt: Asked about France, `tinylm` wrote `a string, and A binascii.Error is raised if`. Which statement about that output is right?
hint: `context used: 1 tokens`.

choices.text: It is random noise, unrelated to the corpus
choices.why: It is the corpus's own most likely text after ` is`.

choices.text: It means the model knew it was wrong and changed the subject
choices.why: There is no signal for that in a distribution.

choices.text: It is what follows ` is` in its corpus, written with no sign that the question was unseen
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It would have been correct with more output tokens
choices.why: More tokens continue the same backed-off text.

prompt: Why is a large model's "I don't know" not enough to tell you when it is reconstructing rather than recalling?
hint: Where does the phrase come from?

choices.text: It is a learnt habit, not a reading of what it knows
choices.why: Right. No internal signal tracks what it learnt.

choices.text: Providers forbid their large models from admitting ignorance in a reply
choices.why: They do say it; the question is when.

choices.text: The phrase appears only at temperature 0, which most applications avoid
choices.why: Temperature does not decide whether a model was trained to say it.

choices.text: The API removes that phrase from replies before they arrive
choices.why: Nothing removes it.

choices.text: Written by the course, chosen by simple rules

choices.text: From a real provider, saved on the day of recording

choices.text: From WordLlama, the lab's embedding model

prompt: A shop wants a model to reply to customers about their own orders. Which design follows from this lesson?
hint: What does the model know about a customer's order?

choices.text: Fine-tune the model nightly on the orders table
choices.why: Training is slow, frozen at its cutoff, and still reconstructs rather than looks up.

choices.text: Ask the model what the customer ordered and check the reply for confidence
choices.why: There is no confidence signal to check.

choices.text: Look the order up in code and put it in the request's context
choices.why: Right. If it is not in the request, the model does not know it.

choices.text: Use temperature 0, so the model cannot invent an order
choices.why: Temperature changes the draw, not what the model knows.
